text: Every owner and group name you saw in the last lesson's ls -l output comes from somewhere. Three plain-text files define every account and group on a Linux system, and this lesson covers how Northbridge's ops team manages its growing roster through them.

Every account has one line in /etc/passwd: username, an x where you'd expect a password, the UID, the primary GID, a comment field, home directory, and login shell. That x matters — the real password hash is never stored here, because this file is world-readable. Linux actually checks the numeric UID and GID internally; the names are just a readable layer on top.

The actual password hash, salted and one-way, lives in /etc/shadow instead, along with password-aging rules like minimum and maximum days between changes. Unlike passwd, shadow is readable only by root, which is exactly why the two files are split apart. That split lets ordinary tools resolve a UID to a username without ever touching anything password-related.

groupadd creates a new group, and useradd creates a user with a home directory, a shell, and supplementary groups. usermod with -aG appends a user to one more group — leave off the -a and you'd overwrite their entire group list instead of adding to it. userdel -r removes both the account and its home directory when someone leaves the team.

Once accounts exist, id and groups tell you what a user actually belongs to: their UID, their one primary group, and every supplementary group on top of it. That's the same group information chmod and chown were acting on back in the last lesson.

You can now trace any username or group name straight back to the files that define it. Next up, lesson twelve: sudo and privilege, how Northbridge's team runs root-level commands without ever sharing the root password.
